text: number 62. Are you solving the wrong constraint? Many entrepreneurs try to fix demand when they actually have a supply problem. Figure out which constraint is real before you throw money at marketing. What are supply versus demand constraints? I see businesses waste countless dollars and time solving the wrong problem. They dump money into ads when they can't handle more customers or obsess over operations when no one's buying. Here's how to diagnose which constraint you actually have and what to do about it. Your business is either supply constrained or demand constraint, never both at the same time. So demand constrained means you have capacity, but not enough customers. Supply constrained means you have customers, but not enough capacity. So here's the test. If you doubled your marketing budget tomorrow, would you double your business or create a nightmare? If nightmare, you're supply constrained. If the business doubled, you're demand constrained. So here are real world examples. Restaurant without empty tables. That would be demand constrained. So fix your marketing. Restaurant with two hour wait time. Supply constraint. Fix your operations to move faster, add takeout, raise prices, or expand. Consultant, fully booked three months out. Supply constraint. Raise prices by at least 50%. Consultant with open calendar slots next week. Demands constraint. Get more leads. Bottom line, businesses that are supply constrained often think they need more customers. They don't. They need more margin, more capacity, or both. Fix with higher prices, more operating leverage. Think better client to provider ratio or tech to speed up delivery, or recruiting to expand capacity. Profit tactic number 63, rush is imaginary. The faster you chase success, the slower it seems to arrive.
